Frame rate

40, 60, 120 and 240 fps: frame interpolation. The game logic keeps its 30 steps a second, and the
frames in between are drawn blended (1 in-between frame per step at 60 fps, 3 at 120 fps,
7 at 240 fps). The display shows at most its refresh rate: higher choices draw that many.
40 fps draws 4 frames for every 3 steps (1 in-between frame per 3 steps), for 40, 80 and
120 Hz screens (a Steam Deck set to 40 Hz or 80 Hz, phones with a 120 Hz panel).
True 60 runs the game logic at 60 steps per second

Your display: %d Hz. 40 fps needs a 40, 80 or 120 Hz screen: here each frame stays on
screen for 1 or 2 refreshes in turn (uneven motion). Choose 30 or 60 fps, or set the
screen to 40, 80 or 120 Hz.
Your display: %d Hz. %d fps needs a %d Hz display; %d fps are drawn (the display cannot show more).
Your display: %d Hz. Frames beyond %d a second are drawn but not shown (presentation without vsync).
Your display: %d Hz
Display refresh rate unknown: %d fps are drawn; frames beyond the display's rate are not shown.

When the computer cannot draw all frames, skip in-between frames instead of slowing the
whole game down. The performance overlay shows how many are drawn.
Off: every logic step waits for all of its frames, so if the frame target is not reached
(e.g. 120/240 fps at a high internal resolution) the whole game runs in slow motion.
Saved separately for 40/60 fps (off by default; on by default on Android and Windows on ARM)
and 120/240 fps (on by default).

Off: if this computer cannot reach %d fps, the whole game slows down (the performance
overlay then shows fewer than 30 logic steps/s). Turn it on to keep the game's speed.

When the device gets hot, 60 fps pauses until it cools down. Relaxed and Off keep 60 fps
longer, but the device may slow down or get warm. Normal suits this device; Relaxed waits
longer on any device; Off never pauses 60 fps for heat.

Debug only, to see how many frames a second this computer can draw: no frame limit and no
vsync. The game counts frames, so it runs faster than normal. The frame rate is in the window
title and the performance overlay. Not saved. (With frame interpolation and Keep game speed
on, the game logic still keeps 30 steps a second.)
Internal resolution
Dynamic resolution

Lowers the internal resolution while the graphics chip cannot keep up with the frame rate, down to
the chosen share of it, and raises it again when there is room. The picture is softer while it is
lower. Helps where the graphics chip is the limit (phones, older computers at a high resolution);
when the processor is the limit, the resolution stays.
Gameplay FOV

100% keeps the original field of view. Higher values show more of the world and make Link
appear smaller. Applies to gameplay and combat in 2D and 3D. Cutscenes, dialogue,
scene transitions and menus keep their authored FOV. First-person view, item aiming and
the Telescope are widened by the same factor, so their zoom is weaker above 100%.
Maximum vertical FOV: 110 degrees. Wider settings also widen visibility/culling checks.

Horizon haze
Default##haze
The pale band low in the sky. 100% matches the original game; lower values give a clearer, deeper blue sky near the horizon. Together with less bloom it gives a more vivid sky. Applies immediately.

Original keeps the game's painted clouds. Toon clouds draws them as puffy cel-shaded clouds with sunlit tops, shaded undersides and banks along the horizon, from the same clouds the game places, so weather and time of day still drive them. Lite is lighter on the GPU (phones, handhelds); High adds self-shadowing.
Soft shadows of the drifting sky clouds on the sea, islands and characters. Weaker at dusk, off at night. Off matches the original game.

A multiplier of 1 leaves that state alone. Boost time is how long a full bar lasts; 0 has no limit, and the bar refills whenever you are not boosting. Cooldown is the bar's refill time (0 for immediate refill). With no limit, or with Show boost bar off, no bar is shown; the boost works the same. The bar also hides while a menu, a cutscene or a conversation is on screen. The dash option replaces the walk clip while boosting; full-speed running already uses dash. Sprint pose adds a forward lean and arm drive while running freely, blended with the boost. Rebind the chosen game button in Controls. Roll, then hold A: roll while running and keep A held as you come out of the roll to boost until you let go. It is always held (Press to toggle does not apply) and works on land only.

Which physical button does each Wii U action. By position: right is A, bottom B, top X and left Y. By label: A does A, B does B, X does X and Y does Y. Automatic reads the connected pad's labels. Button prompts below chooses how those buttons look in the game. Only the four face bindings change.

How the game's button icons look, with any face-button setting. Xbox and PlayStation show the button bound to each Wii U action. By position on Xbox, roll shows B and sword shows A. Automatic follows the connected pad; Nintendo keeps the game's look. By label keeps its existing automatic Xbox fallback. Original keeps the game's look. Custom bindings need four distinct face buttons; otherwise the original icons are used.

How prompts name the shoulder buttons and triggers. Automatic follows the button prompts: LB / RB / LT / RT with the Xbox look, L1 / R1 / L2 / R2 with the PlayStation shapes, the game's L / R / ZL / ZR otherwise. A fixed choice applies with any face buttons setting.
